storyboard.claim: An abused child can be completely invisible across an entire continent — the constant movement is itself the cage.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains icon — bound, imprisoned. Dolores sits trapped on the endless highway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the road's surface freedom (context: picturesque road trip) to its real function as a prison.
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains make the captivity visible; the highway alone could read as freedom.

storyboard.claim: She is trapped in the passenger seat, moving so fast she can never build a life anywhere.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The car — the literal vehicle of her captivity.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms in from the abstract cage to the physical car she cannot leave.
storyboard.addedInformation: The car icon makes the trap concrete: she is a passenger, not a traveler.

storyboard.claim: She has no friends, no teacher to confide in, no money, no one to call.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores alone and slumped — total isolation with no icon, because no single icon captures the breadth of what she lacks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the car that traps her to what the car denies her: any human connection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her slumped body alone on the highway says isolation more honestly than any icon could.

storyboard.claim: Humbert actively engineers her isolation — he uses the legal system as a weapon of terror to control her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Puppeteer icon — one person controlling another. Humbert pointing at Dolores, pulling strings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Dolores's isolation to its architect: Humbert deliberately designs this.
storyboard.addedInformation: The puppeteer makes the control relationship visible — he is the active engineer, not just a bystander.

storyboard.claim: When she threatens to expose him, he threatens her with the Mann Act — a law the audience needs unpacked.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking calmly — the threat delivered as casual conversation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From abstract control to its specific legal instrument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Naming the law on screen anchors the legal jargon the hosts are about to explain.

storyboard.claim: The Mann Act of 1910 made it a federal crime to transport women or girls across state lines for immoral purposes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Law icon in a courtroom — the federal statute being explained.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hosts define the law they just named.
storyboard.addedInformation: The law icon and courtroom set place the viewer in a legal register; 'A FEDERAL CRIME' signals the gravity.

storyboard.claim: The law criminalizes transporting girls across state lines for prostitution, debauchery, or any immoral purpose.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores in the courtroom — she is the girl the law was written to protect.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the legal definition; shifts focus from the statute to its victim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing Dolores instead of Humbert reminds the viewer whose safety this law exists for.

storyboard.claim: Humbert twists the law to convince Dolores that if caught, SHE is the one who will be punished.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing at Dolores — accusing her, reversing the blame.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From what the law says to how Humbert weaponizes it against the very person it protects.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pointing gesture makes the blame reversal physical — he aims the law at her like a weapon.

storyboard.claim: He tells her he might go to jail, but she will become a permanent ward of the state.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking calmly to Dolores — delivering the threat as a rational explanation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies the punishment he threatens her with.
storyboard.addedInformation: The legal phrase on screen makes the institutional threat concrete for the viewer.

storyboard.claim: Humbert's exact threat: she will live with 39 other girls in a dirty dormitory under hideous matrons.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing — delivering his threat with cold precision, quoting himself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The exact words of the threat previewed in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: His own contemptuous word 'dopes' on screen shows how he dehumanizes the girls.

storyboard.claim: His ultimatum: Dolores had better stick to her old man — framing himself as the lesser evil.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing at Dolores, presenting the false choice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The conclusion of the threat: stay with me or face the institution.
storyboard.addedInformation: His phrase 'her old man' on screen exposes the grotesque possessiveness — he calls himself her guardian.

storyboard.claim: The threat makes a 12-year-old believe that the authorities are not her rescue but a worse punishment — her abuser becomes the safe option.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores slumped and worried — she has internalized the trap. No shield icon because the point is protection DENIED.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The psychological result of the threat: she now fears rescue itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the visual mainly repeats her distress; the callout carries the inversion (authorities = punishment).

storyboard.claim: He uses the real bleakness of 1940s welfare institutions to convince her that her abuser is her only protector.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow diagram: GRIM INSTITUTIONS leads to ABUSER AS PROTECTOR — the twisted logic made structural.
storyboard.onScreenText: Flow: GRIM INSTITUTIONS → ABUSER AS PROTECTOR
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Crystallizes the mechanism the last three beats described into a single cause-effect diagram.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flow makes the manipulation's logic legible at a glance — the real bleakness funnels her back to him.

storyboard.claim: When terror is not enough, he bribes her compliance with the cheapest American treats.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding a coin beside Dolores in a diner — the bribe made visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the stick (institutional terror) to the carrot (cheap bribes).
storyboard.addedInformation: The coin in his hand makes the transaction literal: compliance has a price.

storyboard.claim: Sundaes, comic books, nickels for the jukebox — he buys her silence with loose change.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Coin icon — literal money. The cheapness of the bribe.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Itemizes the bribes named abstractly in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The coin icon makes the viewer see the pathetic smallness of what he pays for her captivity.

storyboard.claim: He is buying her silence with loose change and milkshakes while holding the threat of institutionalization over her head.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains icon — she is still bound. Dolores slumped in the diner, controlled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pulls back from the jukebox nickels to the full picture: bribes + threat = captivity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains return from beat 120: the diner is just another form of the same imprisonment.

storyboard.claim: Because of the lyrical prose, the reader gets swept up in the scenery instead of seeing the captive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon — false face. Humbert performing charm, his prose is the mask over reality.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the actual cage (bribes + threats) to how the prose hides it from the reader.
storyboard.addedInformation: Humbert's happy expression beside the mask icon tells the muted viewer: this charm is a performance, not genuine joy.

storyboard.claim: We look at the red bluffs and junipers instead of looking at the hostage in the passenger seat.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores sitting sadly beside Humbert on the highway — the hostage the reader overlooks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The contrast to the previous beat's charming mask: here is what it hides.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's word 'hostage' on screen forces the viewer to see Dolores as a captive, not a passenger.

storyboard.claim: Humbert's prose acts as an opaque veil over the reality of the car.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking neutrally — the veil is his calm, composed narration.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mechanism shown across beats 136–137: the prose is a veil.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the visual mostly repeats Humbert talking; the callout phrase carries the metaphor.

storyboard.claim: To truly read the novel, we must rip the veil away and excavate the real girl trapped inside.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Magnifier icon — close examination. The hosts urge us to look closely at who Dolores actually is.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the veil that hides her to the act of looking past it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The magnifier tells the muted viewer: we are now examining something closely. Dolores's sad face is what the examination reveals.

storyboard.claim: Humbert spends the entire novel trying to bury the real Dolores under an ornamental mythological idea of a nymph.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert talking past Dolores — he narrates over her, burying her in words.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the call to find the real girl to the force working against it: Humbert's narration.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the staging is abstract; the callout's violence ('bury') does the work.

storyboard.claim: Humbert wants us to see a demon child, a fatal creature who seduces him — but that is not true.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores standing ordinary and neutral — NOT staged as a demonic figure. The struck-through callout rejects Humbert's framing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names Humbert's false version of Dolores so the next beat can demolish it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike through tells the muted viewer this label is REJECTED. Dolores's neutral, ordinary posture is the visual counter-argument.

storyboard.claim: Nabokov plants the reality of Dolores in front of us if we care to look past the adjectives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores standing plain beside Nabokov — the author placed her truth in the text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After rejecting the myth, the hosts credit Nabokov for embedding the reality.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing Nabokov beside Dolores distinguishes the author's intent from Humbert's narration — Nabokov planted what Humbert tries to hide.

storyboard.claim: Strip away the poetry and Dolores is desperately, heartbreakingly ordinary — a typical, somewhat awkward American kid.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores standing neutrally in a classroom — an ordinary schoolgirl, nothing mythological.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The answer to 'who is Dolores?' — the opposite of the demon child just struck through.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her neutral expression and classroom setting ARE the point: she looks like any kid in any school.

storyboard.claim: She reads comic books, chews gum, loves jazz and movies — she just wants to be a normal teenager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores happy and holding a book (comic books) in her bedroom — a kid with her interests.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Itemizes the ordinariness named in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her happy face holding a book is the clearest visual of a kid being a kid — the life Humbert stole.

storyboard.claim: Humbert finds her disgustingly conventional — he hates her teenage slang, her real personality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing coldly beside Dolores — his contempt for her ordinariness.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Humbert's response to the ordinary girl the viewer just saw: contempt.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike rejects Humbert's framing — 'disgustingly conventional' is HIS contempt, not the truth about her.

storyboard.claim: Her reality bleeds through his control — especially at the Enchanted Hunter Hotel, their first night together.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores worried, sitting in a bedroom with Humbert — the hotel room where the truth breaks through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Humbert's contempt for her ordinariness to the place where her trauma surfaces.
storyboard.addedInformation: Naming the hotel on screen anchors the scene for viewers who know the novel.

storyboard.claim: Humbert portrays these nights as mutual passion, but the text betrays him completely — he is lying awake waiting to assault her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing blank-faced — NOT staged as romantic. The struck-through phrase rejects his false framing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Inside the hotel: Humbert's version of events, immediately rejected.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike prevents any muted viewer from reading this beat as a romance scene.

storyboard.claim: She sits up gasping, muttering about boats — her arm strikes him across the face in her sleep. Night terrors.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores sitting up in the bedroom, distressed — a child having nightmares.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The text's betrayal: what the mutual-passion claim actually looks like.
storyboard.addedInformation: Humbert's own words on screen — he records the violence of her sleep without understanding what it means.

storyboard.claim: He casually mentions she cries every night when she thinks he is asleep.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores slumped and sad in the bedroom — sobbing into her pillow.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Another detail the text lets slip: from one night's terror to the nightly pattern.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her slumped posture and sad face make the crying visible without sound.

storyboard.claim: Humbert cannot engage with her pain because acknowledging it would destroy his fantasy of a willing participant.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing idle with a blank expression beside Dolores — deliberately not seeing her suffering.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Why Humbert ignores what beats 148–149 just showed: her pain threatens his delusion.
storyboard.addedInformation: His blank neutrality beside her suffering is the visual contrast — he cannot afford to look.

storyboard.claim: When they settle in Beardsley and she interacts with the adult world, the institutions completely fail to see her suffering.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores slumped in a classroom — suffering in plain sight while the school misses it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Humbert's private blindness to the public institutions' identical failure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The classroom set shifts the scene from the private bedroom to the public sphere — same invisibility.

storyboard.claim: The Beardsley school psychologists represent a devastating critique of 1950s institutional psychiatry — they are useless.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores standing anxiously in the classroom — surrounded by an institution that cannot help her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies which institution fails: the school's own psychological apparatus.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the visual is similar to the previous beat; the callout's bluntness does the emotional work.

storyboard.claim: The headmistress calls Humbert in because Dolores is struggling — but they misread the cause.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walking into the classroom with Dolores present — the abuser summoned as the concerned parent.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The institution's attempt to intervene: they call in the wrong person.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing Humbert entering the school makes the irony visible: the predator walks into the rescue meeting.

storyboard.claim: Instead of recognizing the obvious signs of a traumatized, abused child, they hide behind mid-century Freudian jargon.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores sitting sadly — the signs are right there on her face, and the school cannot read them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: What the school sees but cannot interpret correctly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her visible sadness IS the obvious sign — the viewer can see what the institution misses.

storyboard.claim: Miss Pratt tells Humbert that Dolores is shuttling between anal and genital zones of development — absurd Freudian jargon over a kidnapped child.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting with a surprised expression — even the abuser finds the jargon absurd.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The school's actual language, struck through to show the hosts reject it as absurd.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike through tells the muted viewer this clinical phrase is being mocked, not endorsed.

storyboard.claim: They note all the red flags — constant sighing, defiance, dropping grades — but cannot connect them to abuse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores slumped and sad in the classroom — every flag is visible on her body.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the jargon they use to the symptoms they document but cannot read.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her slumped posture embodies the red flags: the viewer sees what the school catalogues but ignores.

storyboard.claim: Their solution: have Humbert — the man raping her — get the family doctor to tell her the facts of life.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting calmly in the school — the institution hands authority back to the predator.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The school's solution to the red flags: astonishingly wrong.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phrase on screen is devastating in context — 'the facts of life' for a child whose life is being destroyed.

storyboard.claim: They have a kidnapped hostage in their classroom and think she just has a bad attitude and needs more group singing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores sitting sadly in the classroom — a hostage they think is merely difficult.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The narrator's reframing of everything the school has missed: this child is a hostage.
storyboard.addedInformation: The harsh phrase 'kidnapped hostage' against the classroom set forces the viewer to see the absurd gap between what she is and how the school reads her.

storyboard.claim: Humbert's respectable, educated European persona completely blinds the American authorities to the monster underneath.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon — false face. Humbert charming and talking with a happy expression in the school — his facade works on everyone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Why the institution fails: Humbert's persona is the mask they cannot see through.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask icon tells the muted viewer his charm is a performance; his happy expression is the lie the school buys.
